clue.text: One's time touring North Dakota with Jack, fine American, though old-fashioned

definitions.note: Only 'fine' is the sense; 'American' and 'though old-fashioned' are usage labels, marking the word as a US colloquialism that has had a dated ring for decades.

indicators.note: A tourist goes round a place rather than into it, so the word it governs travels all the way around the letters named next.

parts.note: j = jack, the card between ten and queen
'one is' contracts to I'm
a day is a measure of time, and it opens up to take the state in
ND is the two-letter postal code for North Dakota

explanation.surface: Someone spends a day driving round North Dakota in Jack's company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One's' looks like a possessive and has to be heard as 'one is'. The jack leads the answer even though the clue mentions him last, after the day out.
explanation.definitionFit: Jim-dandy is American slang for something first-rate, a fine specimen of its kind, and it has sounded quaint since about the 1950s.

clue.text: Juliet Seaman makes punch

parts.note: Juliet is J in the radio alphabet
an AB is an able seaman, the Navy's rating for a trained sailor

explanation.surface: A woman called Juliet Seaman lands one on somebody.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital letters on 'Seaman' are the disguise: it is a rank, not a surname. A jab is thrown with the leading hand and is the shortest punch in boxing.
explanation.definitionFit: A jab is a short straight punch delivered with the front hand, so the plain noun swaps in.

clue.text: Dull-looking, uniform dress in the Middle Ages

parts.note: a mat finish is flat and unshiny, the dull-looking one
Uniform is U in the radio alphabet

indicators.note: What is in the middle of a word is its centre and neither of its ends, so only the inside letters are wanted.

parts.note: the three letters at the centre of dRESs

explanation.surface: Drab, identical clothing of the sort worn in medieval times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Middle Ages' is one phrase on the surface doing two separate jobs underneath: 'in the Middle' hollows out DRESS, and 'Ages' is the definition left standing on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheese, wine and people all mature as they age, so the verb swaps straight in for 'ages' in the same tense.

clue.text: Before noon, work steadily enough

parts.note: am is ante meridiem, the hours before midday
to ply a trade is to keep working away at it

explanation.surface: Putting in a solid stretch of work before lunchtime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Enough' reads as the tail of the sentence about the morning's work and is the definition standing alone. Ply survives mostly in 'plying a trade' and in the plier of oars.
explanation.definitionFit: Amply means to a sufficient degree, so 'paid amply' and 'paid enough' make the same claim.

clue.text: God knows, ultimately, who rigged event where setters may win awards

definitions.text: event where setters may win awards

indicators.note: a rigged contest has been fixed or set up, so these letters are arranged afresh
ultimately picks the final letter of knows

parts.note: last letter of knows

explanation.surface: Heaven knows who fixed the result of a contest for crossword setters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ultimately' takes only the S of knows; 'rigged' then rearranges GOD, S and WHO. 'setters' are not crossword compilers but setter dogs, such as Irish setters.
explanation.definitionFit: At a dog show pedigree breeds, including setter gundogs, are judged and the best win rosettes and prizes.

clue.text: Spoil drop of Courvoisier brandy

parts.note: to mar something is to spoil it

indicators.note: A drop of something is the smallest part of it, which for a word is the single letter it starts with.

parts.note: the opening letter of Courvoisier

explanation.surface: Ruining a small measure of expensive cognac.
explanation.walkthrough: Marc is distilled from the skins and pips left in the press after the wine is made — the rough end of the trade, where Courvoisier sits at the smooth end.
explanation.definitionFit: Marc is a brandy, the spirit French growers distil from pressed grape residue, so the category word defines it.

clue.text: Kind of crack (not heroin) that gets people high?

definitions.note: The definition is a relative clause standing in for a noun — the thing that does this — and it works by what the answer does rather than by any synonym.

indicators.note: Not marks the piece that follows as one to be left out rather than added in.

parts.note: a hairline crack is the finest kind, the one you can barely see
h = heroin in street usage, and it is the letter that goes

explanation.surface: A dealer clarifying which sort of crack is on offer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack' pulls towards drugs and heroin holds you there; the crack wanted is the one in a windscreen. The question mark covers 'high' meaning altitude.
explanation.definitionFit: An airline's business is carrying passengers several miles up, so 'high' is meant literally rather than chemically.

clue.text: Reportedly grab a dal, when served up — it's healthy-ish food

indicators.note: Reportedly means as the thing is said rather than as it is written, so you spell out what the ear receives.

parts.note: to grab is to seize, and 'seize a' said aloud is the emperor's name

indicators.note: In a down clue something served up has been turned over, so its letters are read from the bottom back to the top.

parts.note: dal is the Indian dish of split lentils
as does the work of when in 'as I arrived'

explanation.surface: Someone mishears an instruction to grab a portion of lentils as it arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: Two halves, two devices: the first is a sound, the second a pair of words turned upside down. 'When' pulling its weight as AS is the piece solvers miss.
explanation.definitionFit: A Caesar salad is nominally salad, but the parmesan, croutons and creamy dressing keep it well short of virtuous — hence the hedge.

clue.text: An objection to border

parts.note: an shortens to the single article a
'but' is the word people raise an objection with

explanation.surface: One complaint lodged against a frontier.
explanation.walkthrough: The objection is not described but quoted: 'but' is the word itself, the one that arrives whenever somebody is about to disagree.
explanation.definitionFit: To abut something is to border it, sharing an edge with it, so the two verbs swap in unchanged.

clue.text: Gripping work, being assistant to pianist

definitions.meaning: the book you cannot put down
the person sitting beside the stool at a recital

explanation.surface: An absorbing job helping out a concert pianist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Work' is the hinge: it points at a book, not at employment, and the clue then quietly supplies the employment in its second half.
explanation.definitionFit: A page-turner is a book too gripping to put down, and it is also the recital assistant who turns the sheet music for the player.

clue.text: Fly over to catch a one-time Queen singer in America

indicators.note: the reversed insect catches, holds inside it, the letter a
over means the insect's name is turned over, read backwards

parts.note: a gnat is a small fly
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the late Queen Elizabeth

explanation.surface: An insect flying past is caught by a former royal, who sings in the USA.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to catch' has the reversed fly hold the A inside it. 'singer' suggests a pop star, but here it is a songbird.
explanation.definitionFit: Tanagers are brightly coloured songbirds of the Americas, so a bird singing in America.

clue.text: Bright red tracks alongside Red River

parts.note: Che Guevara, the revolutionary a crossword calls a Red
r = river, as on a map
ry is the short form of railway, whose tracks these are

explanation.surface: Crimson rails running beside a river called the Red.
explanation.walkthrough: A crossword Red is usually a communist, and Che Guevara is the three-letter one. The tracks are named first in the clue but sit last in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Cherry is the vivid red of the ripe fruit, the shade meant by a cherry-red car or lipstick.

clue.text: Our horse goes wild with Bovril — oddly, horses being this?

definitions.note: The setter defines by pointing rather than by synonym: the last three words say the answer is the thing horses are, and the question mark admits the sleight.

indicators.note: Something that goes wild stops keeping to the order it was put in, and letters that go wild land somewhere new.
Oddly points at the odd positions — first, third, fifth — and takes only the letters standing there.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters
the first, third and fifth letters of BOVRIL

explanation.surface: The family horse gets excited at the sight of a jar of Bovril.
explanation.walkthrough: Bovril is the British beef extract stirred into hot water, which is exactly what no horse would touch — the surface contradicts the answer on purpose.
explanation.definitionFit: A herbivorous animal lives on plants alone, which is what horses do: grass, hay, oats and nothing made of beef.

clue.text: In speech, convenient to limit hindrance

indicators.note: In speech means as the word is said rather than as it is written, so the sound is what gets spelt out.

parts.note: convenient is handy, and its sound is written with an i here
a cap is the limit set on a fee or a bonus

explanation.surface: Talk of something convenient that keeps a nuisance within bounds.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the first half is sounded out; the cap arrives spelt as it comes. A cap is the ceiling put on a price or a headcount, nothing to do with hats.
explanation.definitionFit: A handicap is whatever holds you back, so 'hindrance' is the plain noun for the same thing.

clue.text: Weapon that's Spooner's chief boast

indicators.note: Spooner's signals a spoonerism, swapping the opening sounds of two words as the Reverend Spooner did

parts.note: a boss is a chief
to crow is to boast; the spoonerism works on how the words sound, and this one is said kroh

explanation.surface: A weapon described as the Reverend Spooner's chief pride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spooner's' asks for the opening sounds of BOSS and CROW to be swapped, as the Reverend Spooner famously did, giving CROSS BOW.
explanation.definitionFit: A crossbow is a bow mounted on a stock that shoots bolts, a medieval missile weapon.

clue.text: Commotion dogs British party lacking energy and swagger

indicators.note: Something that dogs you comes along at your heels, so this piece trails the letters named after it.
Lacking says a named piece is missing from the word beside it, not added to it.

parts.note: b = British
a rave is an all-night dance party
e = energy, the letter the party loses
ado is a fuss or commotion, as in much ado about nothing

explanation.surface: Trouble follows a British political party that has run out of steam.
explanation.walkthrough: The party the surface offers is a political one and the party wanted is a rave. 'Dogs' is the verb — trouble dogging someone — and it settles which piece trails which.
explanation.definitionFit: Bravado is boldness put on for show with nothing behind it, and a swagger is the same bluster carried in the walk.

clue.text: Rock singles left out to be sorted

indicators.note: to be sorted means put in a new order, so the letters are rearranged
out means the letter for left is removed from singles

explanation.surface: A rock band's singles, with some left out, waiting to be sorted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left out' drops L from SINGLES to give SINGES, and 'to be sorted' rearranges those six letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Gneiss is a coarse banded metamorphic rock, formed under heat and pressure.

clue.text: Area covered by dish which is round or square

indicators.note: Whatever is covered by something has that thing spread over and around it, so the letter goes inside.

parts.note: a pizza is the round dish, and the insertion splits it after two letters
a = area

explanation.surface: A pizza wide enough to blanket the whole area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' belongs to the dish rather than to the shape of the answer, which is the trap. Pizza and piazza differ by one letter, and the clue puts that letter in.
explanation.definitionFit: A piazza is the open public square of an Italian town, the one the cafes and the cathedral face onto.

clue.text: Crash when small weight's upended on head, sustaining stunning blow

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits on top of the next
in a down clue upended means the weight's letters are turned upside down, read bottom to top

parts.note: OZ is the abbreviation for ounce, a small weight; the 's stands for is

indicators.note: the head holds up, sustains, the blow inside itself

parts.note: nut is slang for head
KO is a knockout, a stunning blow

explanation.surface: An accident: a small weight topples onto someone's head and knocks them out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upended' turns OZ into ZO; NUT 'sustaining' KO gives NKOUT beneath it.
explanation.definitionFit: To crash out or zonk out is informal for falling fast asleep from exhaustion.

clue.text: Climb that is followed by walk

parts.note: sc. is the Latin scilicet, the footnote's 'that is to say'
a ramble is a walk taken for pleasure in the country

explanation.surface: A steep ascent with a gentler stroll to follow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That is' looks like the clue's grammar rather than a piece of the answer, which is where the difficulty sits. Scilicet is rarer in print than i.e. but means the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A scramble is a climb up ground rough and steep enough to need hands as well as feet.

clue.text: The foremost of St Andrew's legacies — flag displaying cross

indicators.note: The foremost of anything is what stands at its front, and the front of each word named is its first letter.

parts.note: the opening letters of St, Andrew's and legacies
to flag is to tire, to lose your energy on a long day

explanation.surface: The chief bequest of St Andrew is a flag with a cross on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flag' is the verb, meaning to tire, while the surface keeps it as the thing on the pole. St Andrew was said to be martyred on a diagonal cross, which is why Scotland's flag carries one.
explanation.definitionFit: A saltire is a cross with its arms set diagonally, the heraldic X that Scotland flies in white on blue.

clue.text: Heron flapping after second bird

indicators.note: Something flapping is beating about loose, so its letters will not stay in the order they were given.

parts.note: a mo is a moment, the informal second of 'hang on a mo'

indicators.note: After puts the letters just described behind the piece named next, not in front of it.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 5 letters

explanation.surface: A heron takes off a second behind another bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' is the MO of 'half a mo', not the ordinal. Two waterbirds in one clue, and the big one supplies the letters for the small one.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Bird' is the bare category: the answer is the dark waterbird with the red-and-yellow bill seen on English ponds and canals.

clue.text: County Kerry's neighbour cut large grassy area back

indicators.note: Something cut has had its end taken off, so the last letter of the word named goes.

parts.note: Cork is the Irish county next door to Kerry, cut short by a letter

indicators.note: Back turns the letters just assembled round to read the other way.

parts.note: l = large, as on a clothing label
a lawn is the mown grassy area of a garden

explanation.surface: Trimming a big stretch of grass next door to County Kerry.
explanation.walkthrough: Kerry and Cork are Irish counties and the answer is an English one, which is the jump the clue hides. 'Cut' reads as mowing and means docking a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Cornwall is the county at the south-western tip of England, so 'County' names the category the answer belongs to.

clue.text: Carpets flogged at opening of store, about a hundred

indicators.note: The opening of a word is the letter it begins with and nothing more.
To be about something is to be wrapped round it, so the letters already assembled close over the one that follows.

parts.note: flogged is sold, in the market-stall sense
the first letter of store
C is a hundred in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Rugs going cheap in a shop's launch sale at around a hundred pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carpets' is the British verb: to carpet someone is to call them in and tell them off, a dressing-down on the boss's rug. 'Flogged' is selling, not beating.
explanation.definitionFit: To carpet somebody is British idiom for hauling them in for a telling-off, which is scolding them, and both verbs are third-person singular.

clue.text: Radioed co-ordinates in time for drops

indicators.note: Something radioed arrives as sound over the air, so what you spell is what the ear takes in.

parts.note: to sync things is to co-ordinate them in time, and the word is heard rather than read

explanation.surface: A ship's position is transmitted at the agreed moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Co-ordinates' reads as map references and is the verb, short for synchronises. 'Radioed' is quietly doing the job 'sounds like' usually does.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that sinks drops — the sun sinks behind the hill, prices sink — so the two verbs match in sense and in tense.

clue.text: Moonlit, cool, unending swirls having power to move

indicators.note: What is unending has no end, so the final letter of the word named is taken off.
A swirl spins things round until they settle somewhere new, which is what becomes of these letters.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters
COOL without its last letter

explanation.surface: A cool moonlit night over endlessly swirling water.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma after 'cool' is what tells you 'unending' docks that word and not the swirls. Loco- is Latin for place, the same root that gives the locomotive its name.
explanation.definitionFit: Locomotion is the power of moving from one place to another, the capacity rather than any particular movement.

clue.text: Beautiful goddess imprisoned by the Beast

indicators.note: What is imprisoned is shut inside its surroundings, so the letters sit unbroken within the words that follow.

parts.note: tHE BEast, running across the gap between the words

explanation.surface: Beauty is locked up by the Beast, as the fairy tale has it.
explanation.walkthrough: Beauty and the Beast is the story the surface tells, and the goddess wanted is hiding inside the monster's half of the title.
explanation.definitionFit: Hebe is the Greek goddess of youth, cupbearer to the Olympians, and her name is the word for the bloom of early life.

clue.text: Rotten fish brought up

indicators.note: in a down clue, brought up means the fish's name is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a dab is a small flatfish

explanation.surface: A rotten fish being retched up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought up' looks like vomiting, the effect of the bad fish; in a down clue it tells you to read DAB from the bottom up.
explanation.definitionFit: Food that has gone bad is spoiled or decayed, which is what rotten means.

clue.text: When caught, go down burrow

indicators.note: To catch what somebody says is to hear it, so what is wanted is the sound of the word and not its usual spelling.

parts.note: the sun goes down when it sets, and the sound takes a second t here

explanation.surface: A hunted animal dives underground the moment it is spotted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught' is the homophone signal, in the sense of catching what was said. Badgers are the only British animal whose home takes the doubled spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: A sett is a badger's burrow, the tunnelled chamber system it digs out and lives in for generations.

clue.text: Rise as one, determined, but not fully experienced

indicators.note: Not fully says the words carrying the answer are used only in part, so a run of letters is taken out of the middle of them.

parts.note: riSE AS ONE Determined, straight across the words and the comma

explanation.surface: A crowd gets to its feet together, resolute but holding something back.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing here looks like an anagram or a container, and 'not fully' is the only instruction — easy to read as more of the sentence about being determined.
explanation.definitionFit: A seasoned campaigner is an experienced one: time and use season soldiers and timber alike.
